lesson.subject: anatomy
lesson.title: Brainstem landmarks and crossed findings
lesson.summary: Localization combines level, side and pathway.

steps.title: Brainstem External Anatomy
steps.body: The brainstem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla. It contains cranial nerve nuclei, ascending and descending tracts, reticular formation, and vital autonomic centers.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Midbrain contains cerebral peduncles, tectum, superior/inferior colliculi, and CN III/IV levels. Pons shows basilar pons, middle cerebellar peduncles, and CN V/VII/VIII relations. Medulla shows pyramids, olives, preolivary sulcus for CN XII, and postolivary sulcus for IX/X/XI. Pyramidal decussation lies caudally in medulla. Cerebellar peduncles connect brainstem and cerebellum.

steps.title: Why should sensory modalities be separated when reasoning about a crossed brainstem pattern?
steps.body: Different pathways cross at different levels and occupy different positions. Dorsal-column information crosses in the medulla before ascending as medial lemniscus, while anterolateral pain-temperature pathways have already crossed in the spinal cord. Trigeminal facial sensation has its own nuclei and ascending routes. A lesion can therefore combine facial and body findings with different sides and modalities. Begin with the affected tract and its crossing history rather than applying a blanket rule that all brainstem sensation is contralateral.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Localization combines level, side and pathway. Cranial nerve nuclei or exiting fibers identify a brainstem level; a nearby long tract can produce a deficit elsewhere in the body. Most corticospinal fibers cross in the caudal medulla, so damage above that crossing affects the opposite body side. Sensory tracts cross at different places, preventing a single crossing rule for all modalities. A mixed pattern is a clue to neighboring pathways, not proof of one diagnosis.
